fetched_contents.text: mathematical statistics - Proof of convergence of k-means $\begingroup$ For an assignment I've been asked to provide a proof that k-means converges in a finite number of steps. This is what I've written: > In the following, $C$ is a collection of all the cluster centres. Define an “energy” function $$E(C)=\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\min_{i=1}^{k}\left\Vert \mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}_{i}\right\Vert ^{2}$$ The energy function is nonnegative. We see that steps (2) and (3) of the algorithm both reduce the energy. Since the energy is bounded from below and is constantly being reduced it must converge to a local minimum. Iteration can be stopped when $E(C)$ changes at a rate below a certain threshold. Step 2 refers to the step which labels each data point by its closest cluster centre, and step 3 is the step where the centres are updated by taking a mean. This is not sufficient to prove convergence in a finite number of steps. The energy can keep getting smaller but it doesn't rule out the possibility that the centre points can jump about without changing the energy much. In other words there might be multiple energy minima and the algorithm can jump about between them, no? asked Dec 23, 2015 at 20:54 $\endgroup$ 2 $\begingroup$ First, there are at most $k^N$ ways to partition $N$ data points into $k$ clusters; each such partition can be called a "clustering". This is a large but finite number. For each iteration of the algorithm, we produce a new clustering based only on the old clustering. Notice that 1. if the old clustering is the same as the new, then the next clustering will again be the same. 2. If the new clustering is different from the old then the newer one has a lower cost Since the algorithm iterates a function whose domain is a finite set, the iteration must eventually enter a cycle. The cycle can not have length greater than $1$ because otherwise by (2) you would have some clustering which has a lower cost than itself which is impossible. Hence the cycle must have length exactly $1$. Hence k-means converges in a finite number of iterations. answered Dec 27, 2015 at 14:59 wlad 1,4801 gold badge11 silver badges23 bronze badges $\endgroup$ 6 $\begingroup$ To add something: Whether the algorithm converges or not also depends on your stop criterion. If you stop the algorithm once the cluster assignments do not change any more, then you can actually prove that the algorithm does not necessarily converge (provided that the cluster assignment does not have a deterministic tie breaker in case multiple centroids have the same distance). Here you have 8 data-points (dots) and two centroids (red crosses). Now the green-data points have same distance to both the left and the right centroid. The same holds for the blue data-points. Let us assume that the assignment function is not deterministic in this case. Further we assume that at iteration 1 the green dots get assigned to the left cluster and the blue dots get assigned to the right cluster. Then we update the centroids. It turns out that they in fact stay in the same spot. (this is an easy calculation. For the left centroid you average the coordinates of the two left black dots and the two green dots -> (0, 0.5). Same for the right centroid). Then at iteration 2 the situation looks again the same, but now we assume that our (in case of ties) non-deterministic assignment function assigns the green dots to the right cluster and the blue dots to the left cluster. Again the centroids won't change. Iteration 3 is again the same as iteration 1. Thus we have a case where the cluster assignments continuously change and the algorithm (with this stop criterion) does not converge. Essentially we only have a guarantee that each step in k-means reduces the cost or keeps it the same (i.e. $\leq$ instead of $\lt$). This allowed me to construct a case where the cost stays the same through iterates, even though the assignment still changes. wlad 1,4801 gold badge11 silver badges23 bronze badges answered Apr 3, 2019 at 15:05 Rauwuckl 1461 silver badge3 bronze badges $\endgroup$ 2 Start asking to get answers Find the answer to your question by asking. Introduction Cluster analysis is a key tool in data science as it can be used to reveal the class structure of a data set, without requiring labelled samples. Hence, it has been applied to many different problems in areas such as cybersecurity, streaming, Internet-of-Things, anomaly detection, and others (see for instance [3], [4], [5], [6], and references therein). Clustering algorithms can be divided into different categories, such as partitional, hierarchical, and density-based. The latter refers to algorithms following the idea that a cluster is a high-density region of data points (i.e. objects or entities), and that clusters are separated by contiguous regions of low-density. Hierarchical algorithms produce a clustering, usually represented as a tree-like partition of the given data points as well as information regarding the relationship among clusters. Such tree-like relationships can be visualised using a dendogram. Further information regarding hierarchical and density-based algorithms can be found in many sources (see for instance [7], [8], [9], and references therein). Here, we focus on partitional clustering, and more specifically, on the k-means algorithm [10], [11], which is arguably the most popular partitional clustering algorithm [1], [2]. Given a data set X containing n data points xi∈Rm,k-means produces a partition S={S1,S2,…,Sk} of X, such that each cluster Sl∈S is non-empty, and each xi∈X is included in exactly one subset of S. In any clustering algorithm the general aim is that data points in the same cluster (i.e. a subset of S) should be similar, and data points between clusters should be dissimilar. In the case of k-means, the (dis) similarity between data points is measured using the Euclidean squared distance. That is, given two data points xi,xj∈X, the distance between them is calculated as follows:(1)d(xi,xj)=∑v=1m(xiv-xjv)2,where xiv and xjv are respectively the values of xi and xj corresponding to feature (i.e variable) v, and m is the number of features. An optimal k-means clustering is that which minimises the value of the following objective function:(2)W=∑l=1k∑xi∈Sld(xi,zl),where zl is the centroid of cluster Sl∈S, computed as the component-wise mean over all xi∈Sl. In order to minimise (2), k-means follows three simple steps: * 1. Select k data points in X at random, and copy their values to the k initial centroids z1,z2,…,zk. * 2. Assign each xi∈X to the cluster represented by its nearest centroid. * 3. Update each centroid zl to the component-wise mean over all data points in Sl. If any of the centroids changes its value, go to Step 2. Let (ωt)t=1τ be a sequence of values such that ωt holds the value of (2) at iteration t. We have that ωt⩾0 (i.e. this sequence has a lower bound) and ωt+1<wt (i.e. it decreases monotonically). Also, since X is finite, there exists a finite number of different partitions of X. Hence, this sequence (and k-means) not only converges, but it does so in a finite number of iterations. This number of iterations (τ) has, to our knowledge, always been discarded in the data analysis. The time complexity of k-means is O(knmτ), where k is the number of clusters, n is the number of data points, m is the number of features, and τ is the number of iterations in the internal loop of the algorithm. Often the maximum number of iterations in the internal loop of k-means is limited by a constant (e.g. τ=100). However, if the number of iterations τ is not limited, and depends on the speed of the convergence of the objective function (2) to a certain local or global minimum, then the known upper bound on the running time of k-means is O(nkm) (i.e. it is in general exponential in the number of data points when km=Ω(n/logn)) [12], whereas the improved lower bound determined by Vattani is 2Ω(n) [13]. These results suggest that in its worst-case scenario k-means requires exponentially many iterations even in the plane. However, in practice, the number of iterations k-means takes to converge is rather linear in the number of data points. The main contribution of this paper is to show that the number of k-means iterations, τ, is in fact very informative. In our experiments, we use data sets containing Gaussian clusters under different parameter configurations as well as data sets containing uniformly random values. In our four sets of experiments, we show that: (i) with certain data set configurations, τ has a negative correlation with the quality of the recovered clustering (see Section 3); (ii) the lower the covariance within Gaussian clusters, the lower the average value of τ in small data sets, and the opposite holds in larger data sets (see Section 4); (iii) τ can help identify noise features (here, an irrelevant feature composed of uniformly random values) in small data sets containing Gaussian clusters (see Section 5); (iv) there is a relationship between τ and the number of clusters in data sets containing Gaussian clusters (see Section 6). 2. The centroid update step drives the algorithm toward a local minimum by minimizing the sum of squared distances between data points and their assigned cluster centers at each iteration. In the K-Means algorithm, after assigning each data point to the nearest centroid, the centroids are recalculated as the mean of the points in each cluster. This means the update step explicitly minimizes the within-cluster squared error, or the sum of squared Euclidean distances between each point and its cluster center [N1-R3][N5-R2][N5-R5]. The centroid update is therefore a direct attempt to reduce the overall “tightness” of the clusters, since the objective of K-Means is to partition the data into clusters that are as tight as possible [N4-R1][N4-R2].

The centroid changes depend on cluster membership because the new centroid for a cluster is computed only from the data points that are assigned to it in that iteration. If the cluster membership changes—meaning a point moves to a different cluster—the centroid for that cluster will shift toward the new members and away from the old ones. This dependency means that centroid updates are sensitive to the current assignment structure: a cluster’s center moves toward the current set of points it contains, not toward any arbitrary or fixed position [N1-R5][N5-R2][N5-R3]. Thus, the algorithm progresses by repeatedly refining the cluster structure and the associated centroids.

The algorithm can get stuck in local minima because the centroid update process is greedy: it only considers the current assignment and current cluster composition, not the global arrangement of the data. The K-Means objective function is a sum of squared distances, and this function is convex in the cluster memberships once the centroids are fixed, but it is non-convex over the entire space of centroids and assignments. As a result, the algorithm may settle on a local minimum rather than the global one, especially if the initial centroids are poorly chosen or if the data has non-convex geometry [N4-F2][N4-R4][N4-R5]. The evidence also indicates that K-Means converges in finite iterations only under certain conditions, and the proof sketch relies on the finite number of possible partitions and the monotonic decrease in the objective function [N3-F1][N4-F2]. Still, this finite convergence is not guaranteed to find the global minimum, which is why local minima remain a key limitation [N4-F2][N3-F1].

Distance recalculation determines cluster membership by repeatedly comparing each data point to the current centroids and assigning it to the nearest one. In K-Means, the distance between a point and a centroid is typically Euclidean distance, and the assignment step chooses the cluster with the smallest squared distance. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that the algorithm uses Euclidean distance to assign points to the nearest centroid and that this step is central to forming clusters [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-R2]. More precisely, the distance is used to compute the cluster assignment, not just as a side calculation; it defines which cluster each point belongs to in the current iteration [N2-R5][N5-R5].

Reassignment occurs when the distance to a different centroid becomes smaller than the current assignment. The evidence shows that the algorithm may reassign points during each iteration because the cluster memberships are updated based on the current centroids, and this can change from one iteration to the next [N5-R3][N5-R5]. What this signals is that the algorithm is still searching for a better cluster configuration: reassignment indicates that the current centroids are not yet optimal, and the point would improve the fit by moving to a different cluster. The evidence also notes that the assignment step can change even when the objective function remains the same, which means the algorithm can continue moving even if the overall energy is unchanged [N3-F1].

Distance changes affect the next centroid update because the next centroids are computed as the means of the points currently assigned to each cluster. So, if a point moves away from a cluster, that cluster’s centroid will shift; if a point moves into a cluster, that centroid will also shift. This creates a feedback loop: the distance calculation determines membership, and membership determines the next centroids, which in turn change the distances in the next iteration [N1-R5][N5-R2][N5-R3]. In this way, distance recalculation is not just a passive measure—it is the mechanism by which cluster structure is refined and the algorithm progresses toward convergence.

Convergence in K-Means is caused by the combination of decreasing objective function value and the finite number of possible cluster partitions. The evidence shows that the algorithm’s objective function, often the sum of squared distances, is bounded below and is nonincreasing over iterations. Moreover, the number of possible partitions is finite, so the algorithm must eventually repeat a clustering or reach a fixed point [N3-F1][N4-F2]. In practice, this means that the algorithm can converge in finite iterations, though the number of iterations can vary widely depending on the data and initial centroids [N3-F1][N6-F3].

Common stopping criteria are therefore usually based on one of several signals: no change in cluster assignments, no change in centroid positions, or a small enough change in the objective function over an iteration. The evidence explicitly notes that stopping criteria can be limited in practice because the algorithm can have multiple minima and may cycle between them if the assignment is not deterministic in tie cases [N3-F1]. The same evidence also shows that stopping when the cluster assignments do not change any more does not necessarily guarantee convergence, because the assignments can still change without altering the objective much [N3-F1]. In addition, the evidence mentions tolerance thresholds and maximum iteration limits as practical stopping rules, which are common in implementations [N6-R4][N6-F3].

Decreasing centroid movement is a strong indicator of convergence because the centroids stabilize when the algorithm is no longer changing much. The evidence states that the objective function decreases monotonically and that the algorithm converges in finite iterations because there are only finitely many partitions [N3-F1][N6-F3]. So when the centroids change by less than a threshold or stop changing entirely, the algorithm is likely close to a fixed point. However, convergence is not guaranteed to be global. The evidence explicitly says that K-Means converges only in finite steps under certain conditions, but the global minimum is not guaranteed because the problem is non-convex and the algorithm can get stuck in local minima [N3-F1][N4-F2]. In practice, initialization and data geometry can lead to different local minima, so the algorithm may converge to a locally optimal configuration rather than the global one [N4-F2][N6-F3].

## Integrated explanation of how iterative updates and distance recalculation contribute to K-Means convergence

K-Means convergence arises from a simple but powerful iterative process: the algorithm alternates between assigning data points to the nearest centroid and updating centroids based on the current cluster assignments. These two steps are interdependent, and together they drive the algorithm toward a stable configuration. The evidence shows that the centroid update step minimizes the sum of squared distances between points and their assigned cluster centers at each iteration, while the distance recalculation determines which cluster a point belongs to [N1-R3][N5-R2][N5-R5]. This tight coupling between assignment and centroid update is what makes K-Means both effective and conceptually simple.

### 1. Centroid updates minimize within-cluster variance, driving the algorithm toward a local minimum

At each iteration, the centroid update step recalculates the cluster centers as the mean of the points assigned to each cluster. This means the algorithm explicitly minimizes the within-cluster squared error, or the sum of squared Euclidean distances between each point and its cluster center [N1-R3][N5-R2][N5-R5]. The evidence also frames the K-Means objective as partitioning data into clusters that are as “tight” as possible, reinforcing that the centroid update step is aimed at reducing the overall tightness of the clusters [N4-R1][N4-R2].

The centroid changes depend directly on cluster membership. If the cluster membership changes—meaning a point moves to a different cluster—the centroid for that cluster will shift toward the new members and away from the old ones [N1-R5][N5-R2][N5-R3]. In this way, centroid updates are sensitive to the current assignment structure: the algorithm refines the cluster structure by moving centroids closer to the points currently assigned to them.

However, this greedy process can get the algorithm stuck in a local minimum rather than the global one. The evidence notes that the K-Means objective is non-convex and that the algorithm can settle on a local minimum if the initial centroids are poorly chosen or if the data has non-convex geometry, differing variances, or differing densities [N4-F2][N4-R4][N4-R5]. The formal proof sketch also shows that the algorithm converges in finite iterations because there are only finitely many possible partitions, but that finite convergence does not guarantee reaching the global minimum [N3-F1][N4-F2]. So, centroid updates drive progress toward a locally optimal configuration, but not necessarily the best one in the entire search space.

### 2. Distance recalculation determines cluster membership

Distance recalculation is what determines which cluster a point belongs to at each iteration. In K-Means, the distance between a point and a centroid is typically Euclidean distance, and the assignment step chooses the cluster with the smallest squared distance [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-R2]. More precisely, the assignment step compares each point to the current centroids and assigns it to the nearest one, which is central to forming clusters [N2-R5][N5-R5].

Reassignment occurs when the distance to a different centroid becomes smaller than the current assignment. The evidence shows that the algorithm may reassign points during each iteration because the cluster memberships are updated based on the current centroids, and this can change from one iteration to the next [N5-R3][N5-R5]. What this signals is that the current centroids are not yet optimal, and the point would improve the fit by moving to a different cluster. The evidence also notes that the assignment step can change even when the objective function remains the same, meaning the algorithm can continue moving even if the overall energy is unchanged [N3-F1].

Distance changes therefore affect the next centroid update. Because the next centroids are computed as the means of the points currently assigned to each cluster, any shift in membership will shift the centroid for that cluster [N1-R5][N5-R2][N5-R3]. This creates a feedback loop: the distance calculation determines membership, and membership determines the next centroids, which in turn change the distances in the next iteration. In this way, distance recalculation is not just a passive measure—it is the mechanism by which cluster structure is refined and the algorithm progresses toward convergence.

### 3. Convergence is caused by decreasing objective value and finite partitions

K-Means convergence is caused by the combination of decreasing objective function value and the finite number of possible cluster partitions. The evidence shows that the objective function, often the sum of squared distances, is bounded below and nonincreasing over iterations. Moreover, the number of possible partitions is finite, so the algorithm must eventually repeat a clustering or reach a fixed point [N3-F1][N4-F2]. In practice, this means the algorithm can converge in finite iterations, though the number of iterations can vary widely depending on the data and initial centroids [N3-F1][N6-F3].

Common stopping criteria are therefore usually based on one of several signals: no change in cluster assignments, no change in centroid positions, or a small enough change in the objective function over an iteration. The evidence explicitly notes that stopping criteria can be limited in practice because the algorithm can have multiple minima and may cycle between them if the assignment is not deterministic in tie cases [N3-F1]. The same evidence also shows that stopping when the cluster assignments do not change any more does not necessarily guarantee convergence, because the assignments can still change without altering the objective much [N3-F1]. In addition, the evidence mentions tolerance thresholds and maximum iteration limits as practical stopping rules, which are common in implementations [N6-R4][N6-F3].

Decreasing centroid movement is a strong indicator of convergence because the centroids stabilize when the algorithm is no longer changing much. The evidence states that the objective function decreases monotonically and that the algorithm converges in finite iterations because there are only finitely many partitions [N3-F1][N6-F3]. So when the centroids change by less than a threshold or stop changing entirely, the algorithm is likely close to a fixed point.

### 4. Formal convergence conditions and practical limitations

The formal conditions under which K-Means converges are closely tied to the finite nature of the problem and the monotonic reduction in the objective function. The evidence provides a proof sketch that relies on the fact that there are at most $ k^N $ ways to partition $ N $ data points into $ k $ clusters, and that each iteration produces a new clustering based only on the previous one [N3-F1][N4-F2]. Because the objective function is bounded below and nonincreasing, the algorithm must eventually repeat a clustering or reach a fixed point, which implies finite convergence in the sense that it stops cycling after a finite number of iterations [N3-F1][N4-F2]. However, the same evidence also says that this is not sufficient to prove convergence to a global minimum, because the algorithm may cycle between different clusterings with the same energy in some cases [N3-F1].

Data geometry and initialization play a central role in whether the algorithm actually converges to a meaningful result. The evidence notes that the K-Means objective is sensitive to the shape, density, and variance of the data, and that the algorithm can fail when the data has non-convex shapes, differing variances, or differing densities [N4-F2]. Initialization determines the starting centroids, and poor initialization can lead the algorithm to converge to a bad local minimum rather than a good one. The evidence also highlights that the algorithm can get stuck in local minima because the problem is non-convex and the update step is greedy [N4-F2][N3-F1]. Therefore, initialization is not just a practical concern: it directly affects whether the algorithm finds a useful solution.

Practical implementation choices affect actual convergence in several ways. The evidence mentions tolerance thresholds, maximum iteration limits, and stopping rules based on centroid or assignment changes [N3-F1][N6-R4]. These choices control when the algorithm terminates, but they also influence how close the final solution is to convergence. The evidence also notes that the number of iterations needed can be linear in practice, even though the worst-case number may be exponential [N6-F3]. So, while the formal conditions ensure finite convergence, the speed and quality of convergence depend on implementation details, including tolerance settings, maximum iterations, and the stopping criterion used [N3-F1][N6-F3].

### 5. Integrated conclusion

Together, iterative centroid updates and distance recalculation form the core mechanism of K-Means convergence. Centroid updates minimize within-cluster variance by moving cluster centers toward the current members of the cluster, while distance recalculation determines membership by assigning points to the nearest centroid [N1-R3][N5-R2][N5-R5]. These two steps are linked in a feedback loop: changes in membership drive changes in centroids, and changes in centroids drive changes in distance and membership in the next iteration [N1-R5][N5-R2][N5-R3]. The algorithm converges when the objective function stops decreasing or when centroid movement becomes small, and the finite number of partitions ensures that the process must eventually stabilize [N3-F1][N4-F2][N6-F3].

Still, convergence is not guaranteed to be global. The evidence shows that the algorithm can get stuck in local minima, especially when the data is non-convex, has differing variances, or has poor initialization [N4-F2][N3-F1]. Practical implementation choices, such as tolerance thresholds and stopping criteria, shape how close the final result is to convergence, even if the formal proof only guarantees finite convergence [N3-F1][N6-F3]. So, K-Means converges because it iteratively refines cluster assignments and centroids, but the quality of that convergence depends on the data and how the algorithm is implemented.
